data.targetWord: The Shekhinah is God's manifested glory and presence among his people on earth. It was felt as a pillar of fire or cloud during the Exodus, and dwells in the Tabernacle and Western Wall.

data.sourceWord: God as Creator — stewardship of the earth
data.targetWord: Belief that God created the earth influences Jews to act as stewards, protecting the environment, not abusing resources, and campaigning against global warming, because the earth belongs to God.

data.sourceWord: God as Creator — Shabbat as rest and respect
data.targetWord: God rested on the seventh day of creation; Jews observe Shabbat each week in response, resting to honour God and respect his creation as described in the Torah.

data.sourceWord: Moses — receiver of the Torah and Ten Commandments
data.targetWord: Moses went alone to the top of Mt Sinai to receive the Ten Commandments — a sign of God's covenant with the Jewish people. He is believed to have written the Torah and its 613 mitzvot.
God gave Moses the authority and power to lead the Jewish people out of Egypt, across the Red Sea, and through the Sinai desert, acting as both political and spiritual leader throughout.
'And there has not arisen a prophet since in Israel like Moses, whom the Lord knew face to face.' (Deuteronomy 34:10)

data.targetWord: Shabbat begins at sunset on Friday and ends after nightfall on Saturday. Jews attend synagogue for prayers, light candles, recite Kiddush over wine, and rest from all forbidden work (melacha).

examples.en-GB: AQA Q2.2 — how Jews observe Shabbat

data.targetWord: Shabbat is a time for family, study of Torah, and disconnecting from the working world. It commemorates God's rest on the seventh day and the Exodus from Egypt as an act of spiritual freedom.

examples.en-GB: AQA Q2.2 — how Jews observe Shabbat

data.sourceWord: Synagogue — place of prayer and community
data.targetWord: The synagogue is the central institution of Jewish communal life, providing a place for daily and Shabbat prayer, Torah readings, and life-cycle celebrations in the absence of the Temple.
The synagogue provides Jewish education for all ages, houses the Torah scrolls in the Ark, and offers pastoral and community support — making it essential for preserving Jewish identity.
Pesach (Passover) commemorates the liberation of the Jews from slavery in Egypt. The Seder meal retells the Exodus story using symbolic foods, reinforcing Jewish identity and God's saving power.

Pesach reinforces the covenant between God and the Jewish people. It teaches each generation to see themselves as having personally been freed from Egypt: 'In every generation, each person must see themselves as if they personally left Egypt.'
'And you shall observe this event as a statute for you and for your children forever.' (Exodus 12:24) — commanding Jews to observe Pesach across all generations.

data.title: The Covenant in Judaism
data.sourcePassage: The covenant is a central concept in Judaism — a binding agreement between God and the Jewish people. The first major covenant was made with Abraham: God promised him descendants as numerous as the stars, the land of Canaan, and that he would be the father of a great nation. In return, Abraham and all male descendants were to be circumcised as a sign of the covenant. Later, at Mount Sinai, God made a covenant with all the Jewish people through Moses, giving them the Torah and its 613 commandments (mitzvot). Jews believe that by following the mitzvot, they uphold their side of the covenant. God's side is to protect and bless the Jewish people. The Shekhinah — God's divine presence — is said to rest among the Jewish community when they study Torah and pray together, demonstrating that the covenant remains active. Tikkun olam (healing the world through acts of justice and charity) is one way Jews fulfil their covenant responsibilities today.
